newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN says 3 Iraqi oil deal overseers now in New York.
newsitem.headline: UN says 3 Iraqi oil deal overseers now in New York.

text.p: Three U.N. appointed oil experts, or overseers, arrived at the United Nations on Monday in time for the start of oil contract sales under the oil-for-food accord, the United Nations said.

The three, from Russia, France and the United States were in U.N. headquarters as Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali gave the go-ahead for the plan to be imlemented at a minute past midnight on Tuesday. The fourth, a Norwegian "will be in place Tuesday," said chief U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa.
The overseers must review all oil contracts submitted by Iraq within 24 hours. Two overseers are needed to vet each contract so the approval process can begin before the Norwegian arrives.

Under terms of the deal, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude oil over a six-month period, on a renewable basis, to buy food and supplies for civilians suffering from sanctions imposed after Baghdad invaded Kuwait in August, 1990.
Nearly two-thirds of the oil revenues are earmarked for needy Iraqis, with the balance to pay for Gulf war reparations and other monitoring costs.
A team of 14 people from the the Dutch-firm Saybolt are on the ground in Iraq, charged with monitoring outflows of Iraqi oil at three border stations.
A separate team of 32 personnel from Lloyd's Register will be placed at import facilities in Iraq to ensure only prescribed supplies are brought into the country.
In addition, more than 150 U.N. distribution monitors will work in the country to make sure the food and aid gets to the intended populations.
